title: Fatality inquiry underway; Police witnesses testify woman in cell seemed to be breathing OK before death
article: While it is only verified Colleen Marie Akazay appeared to be alive in her cell at 10:30 a.m. on Feb. 18, 2006 and was found unresponsive 20 minutes later, it is possible she died earlier - unnoticed.
That's according to Pat Brignall, the guard on duty as the 25-year-old was spending her final hours in custody.
Brignall was one of five witnesses testifying in court Tuesday, as a fatality inquiry into the almost three-year-old incident continued.
She said Akazay's stomach rose and fell in a manner quicker than breathing - twitching - during that final check.
"I took it to be breathing," said Brignall.

But she also said, knowing what she knows now from working in a hospital since her time as a guard, bodies can move after death and the movement she saw was not the same as earlier checks. Now she wonders.
Akazay was in custody, with common-law husband Frank Ferguson, after being arrested at Oasis Church for public intoxication that morning.
Three of Tuesday's witnesses - two RCMP members participating in the arrest and a co-ordinator of the shelter run from the church - testified their recollections of the arrest.

"There was a gentleman that came to the doors at about quarter to three and was banging (on them) ... our policy is they have to be in by 12 a.m.," said then-co-ordinator for the winter shelter Sharon Clarkson, who sent a security guard upstairs to inform the man.

"He was up there a while - more than it takes to answer the door - so I went upstairs ... he was still talking to the guy ... he had shut the door and locked it, and the guy was really upset about it ... he was yelling and screaming and kicking."

It was then, said Clarkson, she saw Akazay through the window, sitting against the entrance wall. Both Ferguson and Akazay - in town from Grimshaw - are said to have stayed at the shelter the night prior, but Clarkson did not recognize them.
She called police as Ferguson allegedly became more aggravated.
Const. Helen Pappas was first to arrive, followed by Const. Matt Labelle and Const. Brandy Boychuk.
"I remember seeing a female in the corner ... leaning against the wall, and the male sitting beside her, leaning as well," said Labelle.
"I believe they were trying to go to sleep for the evening ... Const. Pappas was trying to get them up. We assisted her," said Boychuk.

Ferguson is said by Labelle and Boychuk to have been co-operative then, more concerned with his common-law wife being treated well, while Akazay is said to have been more agitated after being roused by the officers.
Clarkson recalls Akazay as unsteady and incoherent, while the RCMP recalls her as steady and coherent enough, at least not out the ordinary given intoxication.
"I don't mean to be blase about it, (she seemed) like another intoxicated person," said Labelle.
Boychuk's testimony echoed this, stating nothing seemed unusual.

Akazay was listed in booking at the detachment, however, as fumbling, falling, incoherent and angry. Pappas brought her and Ferguson in. Labelle and Boychuk went to handle another call before rejoining them.
Multiple bottles of prescription medication and a baggy of powder were found in Akazay's possession.
"It was a baggy of what I first believed was cocaine. It was a (white) powder with a green tinge," said Labelle.
Boychuk said she thought the contents of the baggy looked like crushed pills, assumed to be the same pills found in some of the bottles.
"I don't recall her saying whether she had taken any," said Labelle.
"At the time this was happening, there was nothing that indicated to me that she needed to be anywhere else," said Boychuk.
"She was pretty much the same the whole time."
Intoxicated individuals are normally placed in the drunk tank. Ferguson was, but Akazay was placed in a cell, where she is said to have immediately gone to sleep.

"There were times on weekends when we would get a lot more (prisoners) ... some cells would have six people in them instead of four," said Elaine Hawryluk, the guard on duty when Akazay and Ferguson were brought in.
"We were busy that night and they were bringing in one after the other."
Everything was "fine and dandy," according to Hawryluk, during the span of about 3:30 a.m. when Akazay was booked and 7:30 a.m. when Brignall arrived for the next shift.
Hawryluk checked Akazay every 15 minutes and said she heard her snoring and saw her breathing every time.
"We had a lot in, but there was no really great problem ... I never had any concerns about her at all," said Hawryluk.

But Brignall does not recall hearing the snoring. She said she saw the rise and fall of Akazay's chest, which she took as breathing, and later the quicker, more erratic motions, also taken as breathing.
It wasn't until 10:52 a.m. - a bit past 15 minutes from the last check at 10:30 a.m. - while she was doing rounds with Sgt. Ross Gear, when the situation was discovered.
"I was walking in behind (Sgt. Gear). He knocked on the cell and called her name but she didn't respond, so he went inside the cell and shook her. She didn't respond," said Brignall.
CPR was performed, first by Gear and then by Emergency Medical Services upon their arrival, but "to no avail," said Brignall.
Akazay was pronounced dead.
Toxicology reports would later reveal Akazay died from a combination of alcohol and very high levels of prescription painkillers and sedatives.
The codeine alone detected in her blood was nearly twice as high as what would be considered lethal.

Raised on Tuesday was the question of why the situation was not recognized for what it was - by RCMP members or either guard on duty - with the pill bottles and baggy of powder having been discovered and documented.

Also raised was the question of why Brignall's paperwork had the usual checkmarks next to Akazay's name, verifying she was still all right at each check, but not Brignall's initials in several instances.
Brignall clarified they were her checks, but offered little explanation as to why she didn't initial them other than "stupidity" in the midst of a very busy shift.
The fatality inquiry will continue today, when just two more witnesses are expected to testify.
